# How This Book Is Being Written {.unnumbered}

A book about AI-assisted engineering should be candid about how it was made.
This manuscript is being developed in the open while both the subject and the
text are still taking shape. I chose that openness deliberately. I do not want
to write about how AI changes engineering only from a distance. Working with
these systems every day has made both their leverage and their failure modes
harder to romanticize. The public draft lets me test the argument against
current research, working systems, and critical readers rather than waiting for
the field to settle. Its status as a development build is not an excuse for weak
claims. It is an opportunity to find them early. Thinking in the open also gives
me a reason to keep the evidence and examples current as the field changes.

The process described in this book is also how I am writing it. I formulate a
question, explore alternatives, implement a draft, evaluate it against sources
and what readers need from the chapter, interpret what failed, and decide what
to retain or revise. The correspondence is not exact. Writing a synthesis
lecture is not the same as designing a chip, and it does not produce physical
measurements or validate the book's technical claims. Both kinds of work still
require the current state, the checks applied to it, and responsibility for the
resulting decision to remain visible.

I use generative AI systems throughout this work. Models and tool-assisted
workflows help me propose outlines, surface adjacent work for closer reading,
generate alternative explanations, challenge assumptions, critique drafts,
check consistency, and write or debug supporting code. Their greatest value is
breadth. They can quickly produce candidate organizations, connections,
counterarguments, and explanations that would take much longer to assemble by
hand. That breadth also creates a review problem. Fluent material can
accumulate faster than its assumptions, sources, and implications can be
checked.

The process also clarified what synthesis requires. Generative systems can
supply breadth, candidate connections, counterarguments, and even possible
syntheses. They do not decide which perspective this book will defend. That
requires choosing which distinctions matter, what evidence supports a claim,
where an analogy fails, what belongs in the argument, and what should be left
out. My role is not a final approval step after generation is complete. I frame
the questions, select and interpret the evidence, connect the ideas, challenge
fluent but weak reasoning, and decide what the book says. I remain responsible
for those decisions and for the integrated result.

I learned this most clearly when I allowed output to outrun review. The prose
became smoother while the argument became weaker. Sections accumulated
repeated concepts, attractive terms without clear meanings, and citations that
did not always support the precise claim being made. Repairing those failures
required returning to the purpose of the chapter, checking the sources again,
and sometimes discarding substantial changes. More generation did not remove
the need for judgment. It increased the amount of material that required it.

The tools also made it easier to examine ideas from computer architecture,
machine learning, electronic design automation, software engineering,
experimental science, and systems safety together. Collecting those ideas is
only the beginning. The harder work is deciding what transfers, what breaks
under architecture constraints, and what coherent perspective remains.
Writing the book has made that distinction more concrete for me.

Writing is also how I test whether I understand a subject well enough to teach
it. When an explanation cannot survive a reader's questions, the synthesis is
not finished.

This remains a working manuscript, and I expect it to change as the argument
and evidence improve. Publishing it in the open does not transfer
responsibility to you, but it gives you an opportunity to challenge the work
before it settles. If you find a passage that is vague, imprecise, or wrong, or
a connection that deserves a harder test, I would genuinely like to hear it.
Feel free to [reach out](https://vijay.seas.harvard.edu).

Vijay Janapa Reddi
